summary: This unit teaches you to help prepare, carry out and review the operational plan for an electrical contractor's crew. You will learn how the plan links to the company's strategy, how to write SMART objectives and KPIs, how to work out the people, equipment, materials and money the plan needs, how to monitor progress with simple figures and budgets, how to manage risks and changes, and how to report and review so the next plan is better.

blocks.p: A company that only reacts to each day's jobs soon runs out of people, vans, breakers or cash at the worst moment. An **operational plan** says, for the next few months, what work the crews will do, with what, by when, at what cost and how success will be measured. As a Level 3 lead electrician you do not write the whole plan, but your input on how long jobs take and what the crew needs is what makes it realistic, and your crew delivers it.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Describe how the operational plan turns the company's strategic (business) plan into the crew's work, and the lead electrician's part in it.
Write SMART objectives and choose key performance indicators with targets, time periods and data sources.
Collect the crew's knowledge of real job times, risks and needs, check it against data and pass it on.
Calculate labour hours, compare them with hours available, list materials, tools, vans and test instruments, and cost them in J$.
Read a budget, work out variances in J$ and per cent, and tell favourable from adverse.
Use a Gantt chart or job schedule with milestones, and decide the order of jobs by safety, urgency and contract.
Use job sheets to compare actual results with the plan each week, work out rates and percentages, find causes of shortfalls and report with proposed actions.
Keep a risk register with ratings, controls and owners; re-plan when clients, staff or suppliers change things; record changes in a change log.
Keep to law, policy and ethics
Never let the plan cut safety, testing or supervision; protect records; keep figures honest.
Help review the plan at the end of its period so lessons go into the next one.

blocks.note: Prices in this kit are in Jamaican dollars (J$). Quotations to clients add GCT at the current rate; the plan's budget says whether its figures are with or without GCT. All sums in the examples are worked out in full so you can check them. Work every sum twice.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Level
Who
Looks ahead
Answers
rows: Where is the company going? Which markets (housing, hotels, solar, maintenance)? Mission, vision, values.
A year or less, often by quarter
Who does which jobs, with what people, equipment, materials and money, by when, and how we measure it.
Which crew is on which site on which day; what is needed on the van.

blocks.p: The operational plan is how a strategy becomes real. If the strategy says 'double our maintenance contracts in three years', the operational plan for this half-year says, for example: win four new contracts, train two electricians in air-conditioning controls, buy a second service van, and answer 90% of breakdown calls within four hours.

ul: The **objectives** for the period and the **KPIs** that measure them.
The **work**: jobs, contracts and maintenance visits expected.
**Resources**: people (and their skills), vans, tools, test instruments, materials and subcontractors.
The **budget**: expected income and costs by month.
The **schedule**: who does what, when, with milestones.
**Risks** and what will be done about them.
How progress will be **monitored**, **reported** and **reviewed**, and who is responsible for each part.

blocks.h: Tools used when the plan is prepared

head: Tool
What it does
rows: Lists the company's Strengths and Weaknesses (inside) and the Opportunities and Threats (outside), for example: strength, licensed inspectors on staff; weakness, no solar experience; opportunity, new housing schemes; threat, copper prices and theft.
The real hours, materials and callbacks from past jobs: the best base for new estimates.
The views of the crew, stores, office, clients and suppliers.
The leave roster and training calendar
Who will not be available, and when.

ul: Gives honest estimates of how long jobs take, from job sheets, not guesses.
Says what the crew needs: tools, testers, van stock, training.
Points out risks: skills gaps, old equipment, one supplier for a key item.
Collects and passes on the crew's ideas and concerns.
Once the plan is agreed, explains it to the crew, leads them to deliver it and reports progress.

head: Letter
Test
Weak
SMART
rows: A handover checklist and torque screwdrivers on every van
Paint the vans a new colour
Fewer callbacks means lower cost and happier clients
By the end of the second quarter

blocks.p: A **KPI** is a number that shows whether an objective is being met. Each needs a **target**, a **time period**, a **data source** and a **named person** who reports it.

head: KPI
Target (example)
Where the data comes from
Why it matters
rows: Inspection results on the job files
Failures cost return visits and delay the client's connection.
Below 3% of completed jobs a quarter
Job log of returns to fix faults
Shows workmanship; callbacks are unpaid labour.
Jobs completed by the agreed date
Shows whether planning and resources work.
Lost-time injuries and near misses reported
Zero injuries; all near misses reported
Safety first; near-miss reports show a healthy culture.
Shows whether estimates are right and crews are productive.
Each stock-out means a wasted trip.

ul: A KPI must be **collected the same way every time**, or the trend means nothing.
Too many KPIs and nobody looks at any: four to six good ones are enough for a crew.
Measure what matters, not what is easy. Hours on site measures effort, not results; the pass rate measures results.
Show the KPIs where the crew sees them: a chart on the workshop wall with the target line, updated weekly.

blocks.h: Consulting the crew and other stakeholders

blocks.p: **Stakeholders** are the people the plan affects or who affect it: the crew, the stores, the office, clients, suppliers, subcontractors and, for some jobs, the licensed inspector. Consulting them before the plan is fixed finds problems early and makes people more willing to deliver the plan.

head: Ask
Not
rows: What could stop us meeting these targets, and what would help?
Do you all agree the targets are fine?
How long does a typical two-bedroom rough-in really take you? Show me a recent job sheet.
Which items do we run out of on the van?
Why do you keep running out?

blocks.p: When an experienced crew member says the plan allows too little time, do not dismiss it and do not simply accept it: check the claim against past job sheets and report what the data shows. The plan is then based on evidence, and the crew sees that its views count.

flow: List the jobs in the period with the estimated labour hours for each, from past job sheets
Add them up by month: the hours needed
Work out the hours available: electricians × working hours per month, less leave, training and public holidays
Compare: the gap is the shortfall or the spare capacity
Decide how to close a gap: approved overtime, a temporary electrician, a subcontractor, moving jobs, or re-planning dates with clients

blocks.p: **Worked example.** Next month the crew must wire 8 flats at 60 hours each and do 220 hours of maintenance visits. Hours needed: 8 × 60 = 480, plus 220 = **700 hours**. The crew has 5 electricians, each with 8 hours a day for 21 working days = 168 hours; one is on leave for 5 days (40 hours) and all five have a day of training (5 × 8 = 40 hours). Hours available: 5 × 168 = 840, less 40, less 40 = **760 hours**. There is spare capacity of 60 hours, but that is only 8%, so a sick day or a late delivery would use it up.

**Worked example.** A contract needs 1,350 labour hours over three months. Each electrician gives about 150 productive hours a month, so 450 hours over the period. 1,350 ÷ 450 = **3 electricians** for the whole three months. If only two can be spared, the gap is 1,350 − 900 = 450 hours; at overtime of J$1,800 an hour that would cost 450 × 1,800 = J$810,000, so a temporary electrician may be cheaper.

blocks.note: A working day has 8 paid hours, but not all of them are productive. Travel, loading the van, toolbox talks and waiting for access can take 1 to 2 hours a day. Estimate with the **productive** hours per day the job sheets show, and plan travel time separately. Grouping each day's jobs by area cuts the travel.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Compare the skills each job needs (solar PV, fire alarms, motor controls, high-voltage work) with the skills the crew has. A gap is closed by approved training booked **before** the work starts, by hiring, or by a subcontractor while the crew learns alongside. Never plan for an untrained person to do specialist work, and never plan for a trainee to work unsupervised or live.

ul: List the vans, ladders, platforms, power tools and test instruments, with service and **calibration due dates**.
Book calibration early and arrange a calibrated spare, so testing never stops because the only tester is away.
Plan van servicing in quiet weeks, and know what happens to the schedule if a van is off the road.
Hire or share large items (a scissor lift, a cable puller) rather than buy them for one job, unless the sums say otherwise.
Take off the materials for a typical job from its drawings, multiply by the number of jobs, and add an allowance for waste and damage (often 5 to 10% for cable, less for fittings).
Note items with long **lead times** (panels, switchgear, special luminaires) and order them in time.
Set a **minimum van stock** for common items (breakers, outlets, boxes, clips, tape) and a **reorder point**: when stock falls to it, reorder.

Reorder point = daily use × lead time in days + a safety stock. **Example**: a crew uses about 6 single-pole 20 A breakers a day; the supplier takes 3 days; safety stock 10. Reorder point = 6 × 3 + 10 = **28** breakers.
Count the van stock weekly against the list.

blocks.p: A **budget** is the planned amount of money for each heading over a period: income expected, and costs by type and by month. The lead electrician helps by giving realistic labour and material figures, and by watching actual costs against the budget.

head: Type
Meaning
Electrical examples
rows: Stays the same whatever the amount of work
Workshop rent, insurance, van loan payments, office salaries, licences
Rises and falls with the work done
Cable and fittings used, fuel for each job, overtime, subcontractors
Can be charged to one job
That job's materials and the hours worked on it
Rent, the stores clerk, calibration, phones

blocks.p: A **variance** is the difference between the budget and the actual figure. For a cost, under budget is **favourable**; over budget is **adverse**. For income, above budget is favourable. Variance % = variance ÷ budget × 100.

The total is exactly on budget, yet the month has two real problems. Labour is 8% over (overtime? rework? estimates too low?) and transport is 15% over (extra trips? fuel price?). The materials saving may be good news, or it may mean that jobs are behind and the materials have not been used yet, or that a supplier has not yet invoiced. **Always look inside the total and check favourable variances too.**

A good variance report gives the figures, the likely **cause** and a **proposed action**: 'Transport J$30,000 (15%) over: 14 extra trips to the wholesaler for items missing from the vans. Proposed action: minimum van stock list and weekly check from next week.' Managers can then decide quickly.

If the price of copper cable or fuel rises sharply during the plan period, report the effect on the remaining jobs at once and suggest options: re-quote future jobs, buy ahead for confirmed jobs, or agree price changes with clients where the contract allows. Never use a thinner cable than the design states to save money.

Profit on paper does not pay wages this Friday. **Cash flow** is the timing of money in and out. A job that needs J$900,000 of switchgear now, with the client paying 60 days after completion, can leave the company unable to pay its supplier or its staff. The plan arranges a **deposit** or **stage payments** on large jobs, chases invoices promptly, and uses supplier credit terms. **Mark-up** is added to cost to set a price: a job costing J$400,000 with a 25% mark-up is priced at 400,000 × 1.25 = J$500,000 before GCT.

A **Gantt chart** shows each job or task as a bar along a time scale, so everyone can see who is where each week and where jobs overlap. A **milestone** marks the end of a key stage, such as 'rough-in complete', 'board energised' or 'inspection passed'. Milestones show quickly whether the job is on track. A **critical** task is one that delays the whole job if it slips, such as the switchgear delivery.

When two jobs compete for the same morning, decide by **safety risk, urgency and contract terms**, not by who pays more or which job is closer. A clinic without power in a treatment room comes before new display lights for a shop. Maintenance contracts often promise a response time, and that promise is part of the plan.

blocks.h: Monitoring: where the numbers come from

blocks.p: **Job sheets** filled in every day (hours, materials, test results, problems, waiting time) are the raw data for everything else: KPIs, variances, estimates for the next plan and the client's invoice. A job sheet filled in from memory on Friday is guesswork.

head: Measure
How
Example
rows: 72 outlets in 24 hours = 3 outlets an hour
Paid hours when the crew could not work
3 electricians waiting 2 hours for a delivery = 6 hours lost
% of work done compared with % of time gone
35% done with 50% of the month gone: behind

flow: Collect the week's job sheets and check they are complete
Work out the KPIs and compare them with the targets and the schedule
Update the KPI chart where the crew sees it
Hold a short crew meeting: results, causes, actions
For each shortfall, find the cause (not the person to blame): late materials, rework, wrong estimate, sickness
Agree a corrective action with an owner and a date
Report upward what is beyond your authority, with figures and options
Next week, check whether the action worked

blocks.p: **Example.** The first-time pass rate has fallen for two months. Changing the target, or warning the crew, fixes nothing. Reading the inspection failure reports shows that most failures are missing labels and missing test certificates. A handover checklist signed by the lead before the inspection is booked removes the cause.

ul: A weekly progress report holds: jobs done against the plan, hours and spending against the budget, KPI results, issues, actions and what is needed from the manager.
A report on a missed KPI includes the cause and a proposed action.

Test results, client details and staff information are kept **password-protected** on the company system, backed up, and seen only by those who need them. Do not copy them to personal phones or pin them on notice boards.
Keep the **change log**: each change to the plan, the date, the reason and who approved it.

blocks.p: A **risk** is something that might happen and would harm the plan. The **risk register** lists each risk with its likelihood, its consequence, a rating, the controls, a contingency and an owner. A common scoring is **likelihood (1 to 5) × consequence (1 to 5)**, so ratings run from 1 to 25; deal with the highest first.

head: Risk
L
C
Rating
Control (reduce the chance or the harm)
Contingency (what we do if it happens)
Owner
rows: Hurricane or tropical storm stops site work (June to November)
Schedule roof and outdoor work early in the season; stores off the floor; vans fuelled
Secure sites at a warning; priority list of clients for repairs after
Deliver just in time; lock cable away; no cable left overnight
Report to police; insurance; replacement stock
Only one person trained on fire alarm systems
Train a second person before the job
Order early; confirm delivery weekly; second supplier identified
Re-sequence the job; tell the client early
Tester out of calibration during a busy month
Client pays late on a large job
Deposit and stage payments in the contract

blocks.p: A **control** acts before the event to make it less likely or less harmful. A **contingency** is the plan for what to do if it happens anyway. 'Hope it does not happen' is neither.

blocks.note: The hurricane season runs from June to November, with the busiest months usually August to October. Plan for storms stopping work, flooded stores, power and phone outages, ports and suppliers delayed, staff unable to travel, and a rush of urgent repair calls afterwards. At a warning, crews make sites safe: isolate temporary supplies, secure materials and ladders, protect open panels. Afterwards, flooded equipment is checked before it is energised, and clinics, water pumps and cold stores come first.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Use the **leave roster** at the planning stage so two key people are not away in the same busy week.
A new electrician gets an **induction** on the first day: safety, rules, the people and their role; then supervised work.
Record each person's training and certificates, and their renewal dates.

blocks.h: Managing a change to the plan

flow: Get the change in writing: new dates, scope, any penalty or bonus
Check the schedule for clashes and the labour hours needed in the new period
Check material lead times and equipment availability
List the options: move less urgent jobs (with those clients' agreement), approved overtime, temporary staff, split the crew, subcontract
Cost each option in J$ and check its effect on safety and quality
Take the options to the manager for a decision
Update the schedule and the change log; tell everyone affected: crew, stores, other clients
Watch the KPIs over the next weeks

blocks.p: When a client moves a date, **everyone affected** is told: the crew, the stores (so materials move with the job), the manager and any other client whose job shifts. A van off the road for a week means checking the schedule and arranging cover or re-planning, not cancelling the week or borrowing someone's private car.

sections.title: Law, policy and ethics in the plan

blocks.p: A plan that meets its targets by cutting safety, skipping tests or faking records is a failed plan, whatever the KPIs say. The lead electrician is often the person who sees this first.

head: Pressure
The right response
rows: The draft plan has a trainee testing alone at a live board to save hours
Raise it and change the plan: trainees work dead, supervised. Live testing is for competent, authorised people.
The crew is behind and wants to skip the final tests to catch up
Refuse. Testing proves the installation is safe and the certificate true. Fix the delay instead: find its cause and report options.
A client wants the GFCI or RCD left out to save money
Explain why it is required and keep to the specification and the code the Centre uses.
A colleague asks you to sign test results you did not see taken, to meet a KPI date
Refuse and report that the tests are not done. A false record hides the problem and may be illegal.
A crew member is asked to work hours that break the company's rules on rest
Fatigue causes accidents; re-plan the work or get more people.

ul: The plan must keep to employment law (hours, overtime pay, leave), safety law and the company's policies.
A new or altered installation must pass the licensed inspector before JPS connects it; build the inspection and the certificates into the schedule.
Keep KPI figures honest. A rate that looks good because failures were not recorded stops the real problem being fixed.
Treat clients' details and staff records as confidential.

blocks.p: At the end of the period, gather the KPI results against targets, the budget against actual spending, jobs completed against the schedule, which risks happened, and the crew's and clients' views. Pick out what went well and what went badly, find the causes, and propose specific changes for the next plan: better estimates from real job sheets, new or changed KPIs, training, a second supplier, different stock levels. Write it down, share it with the crew and keep it, so the lessons are not lost.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can explain the difference between the strategic plan, the operational plan and the weekly schedule, and the lead electrician's part in each.
I can list what an operational plan contains and explain a SWOT analysis.
I can write a SMART objective and choose KPIs with targets, periods, data sources and owners.
I can consult the crew in a way that gets useful answers, and check their claims against data.
I can work out labour hours needed and available, the gap, and the cost of closing it.
I can identify skills gaps and the ways to close them before the work starts.
I can plan equipment, calibration, materials, lead times and reorder points.
I can tell fixed from variable and direct from indirect costs.
I can work out variances in J$ and per cent, say whether they are favourable or adverse, and look inside the total.
I can explain cash flow, deposits, stage payments and mark-up.
I can read a Gantt chart, use milestones and decide the order of jobs.
I can work out completion, pass, callback and productivity rates from job sheets.
I can run a weekly review, find causes and agree actions with owners and dates.
I can keep a risk register with likelihood × consequence ratings, controls, contingencies and owners.
I can plan for the hurricane season and for staffing risks.
I can manage a change to the plan and keep a change log.
I can refuse plans that cut safety, testing or honesty, and explain why.
I can help review a plan so the next one is better.

head: Formula
Use
rows: Hours needed = jobs × hours per job (+ other work)
Hours available = people × hours each − leave − training − holidays
Variance = actual − budget; variance % = variance ÷ budget × 100
Reorder point = daily use × lead time + safety stock

terms: A cost over budget, or income under budget.
The planned amount of money for each heading over a period.
The timing of money coming in and going out.
The record of each change to the plan, with the date, reason and who approved it.
What will be done if a risk happens.
An action taken in advance to make a risk less likely or less harmful.
Paid time when the crew cannot work, for example waiting for materials.
A cost under budget, or income over budget.
A cost that stays the same whatever the amount of work.
A chart showing tasks as bars along a time scale.
General Consumption Tax, added to quotations at the current rate.
Key performance indicator: a number that shows whether an objective is being met.
The time between ordering an item and receiving it.

c1.title: A half-year plan at a Linstead contractor
c1.text: Ricardo Mullings is lead electrician at a contractor in Linstead, St Catherine, whose business plan aims to grow its maintenance contracts with cold-storage and poultry farms. The manager asks Ricardo to help draft the operational plan for January to June. His crew currently answers breakdown calls in anything from two hours to two days, and its first-time inspection pass rate on new work has been 80% for a year.

c2.title: Staffing a church hall and a townhouse scheme in Mandeville
c2.text: A contractor in Mandeville, Manchester, has won the wiring of 10 townhouses at 70 labour hours each, to be done over two months alongside 300 hours of existing maintenance work. The crew has 4 electricians, each available for 160 hours a month. One electrician will be on leave for 10 days (80 hours) in the first month. Overtime costs J$2,000 an hour; a temporary electrician would cost J$280,000 a month.

c3.title: A monthly budget review in Santa Cruz
c3.text: Tanya Blake, lead electrician at a contractor in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth, reviews last month's figures with the manager. Labour: budget J$1,200,000, actual J$1,290,000. Materials: budget J$1,800,000, actual J$1,650,000. Transport: budget J$180,000, actual J$207,000. The material saving puzzles the manager, because two jobs were delayed waiting for luminaires that have still not arrived.

c4.title: A June change card in Port Maria
c4.text: Jerome Barrett leads a crew for a contractor in Port Maria, St Mary. On a Monday in June, three things happen at once: the only electrician trained on the hotel's fire alarm system goes off sick for two weeks; a supermarket client asks for its refit to start two weeks early; and the panel supplier says a switchboard ordered for a school will be three weeks late. The crew's risk register, written in January, scores likelihood and consequence from 1 to 5.

c5.title: Watching the KPIs at a Black River contractor
c5.text: Jodi-Ann Reid is lead electrician at a contractor in Black River, St Elizabeth. This month's job sheets show: 36 jobs completed of 40 planned; 19 of 20 new installations passed inspection first time; 5 callbacks on 125 completed jobs; and the crew fitted 96 light points in 32 working hours. Halfway through the following month, only 30% of that month's jobs are complete. A colleague suggests leaving two callbacks off the log 'because they were small'.

questions.q: Ricardo's first draft objective for the farm contracts says 'Improve our response'. Which rewrite is SMART?
o: Respond to farm breakdown calls much faster over the coming months
Answer 90% of farm breakdown calls in 4 hours, every month until June
Be the quickest responder to farm breakdowns in all of Jamaica
Always answer farm breakdown calls as fast as the crew can manage
questions.why: It is specific (farm breakdown calls), measurable (4 hours, 90%), achievable with planning, relevant to growing maintenance contracts, and time-bound (each month to June). 'Faster', 'quickest' and 'as fast as possible' have no number, and two have no date.

questions.q: Ricardo wants a KPI for the quality of the crew's new installation work. Which is best?
o: The number of hours the crew spends on each new installation
The amount of cable and fittings bought for new work each month
The number of jobs the crew starts in each month of the plan
The share of new installations passing inspection first time
questions.why: A KPI should measure the result that matters. The first-time pass rate shows the quality of the finished work; hours, materials and jobs started measure effort or activity, not quality. The data comes from the inspection results on the job files.

questions.q: Before the plan is fixed, the manager wants Ricardo to find out from the crew how long a poultry-house rewire really takes. What should he ask for?
o: Their honest guess, in a short meeting, of the hours a rewire needs
The hours on two or three recent job sheets, and why any job ran long
Whether the crew would rather have longer or shorter hours per job
A promise that each rewire will be done inside the hours in the draft
questions.why: Consultation should bring evidence. Recent job sheets give real hours and the reasons for overruns, which the plan can use. Guesses, preferences and promises do not tell the planner how long the work takes.

questions.q: A senior electrician says the plan's 70 hours per townhouse is too few. What should Ricardo do?
o: Check the claim against past job sheets and report what they show
Keep 70 hours, because the plan has already gone to the manager
Raise the estimate to whatever the senior electrician asks for
Lower his workload so that the complaint does not come up again
questions.why: Consultation means checking the crew's knowledge against evidence. Past job sheets show the real hours; Ricardo reports the data and lets the plan be based on it. Dismissing the claim or accepting it without checking both lead to a weaker plan.

questions.q: How many labour hours does the crew need over the two months, and how many does it have?
o: Needs 1,000 hours; has 1,280 hours
Needs 700 hours; has 1,200 hours
Needs 1,300 hours; has 1,280 hours
Needs 1,000 hours; has 1,200 hours
questions.why: Needed: 10 × 70 = 700, plus 300 maintenance = 1,000 hours. Available: 4 × 160 × 2 = 1,280, less 80 hours of leave = 1,200 hours. The crew has 200 hours of spare capacity over the period, but check the first month on its own, where the leave falls.

questions.q: In the first month alone, 600 of the hours are needed. How does the first month look?
o: 560 hours available, so about 40 hours short
640 hours available, so about 40 hours spare
480 hours available, so about 120 hours short
600 hours available, so exactly on balance
questions.why: First month available: 4 × 160 = 640, less 80 hours of leave = 560 hours, against 600 needed, so 40 hours short. Spare capacity over the whole period can hide a shortage in one month; plan month by month.

questions.q: The lead suggests covering the first month's 40-hour gap with overtime. What would it cost, and is a temporary electrician cheaper?
o: J$80,000; the temporary electrician at J$280,000 costs more
J$20,000; the temporary electrician at J$280,000 costs more
J$80,000; the temporary electrician at J$280,000 is cheaper
J$280,000; both options cost the same amount
questions.why: 40 hours × J$2,000 = J$80,000. A temporary electrician for the month costs J$280,000, so for a gap this small, approved overtime is the cheaper option. If the gap were 150 hours (J$300,000 of overtime), the temporary electrician would be cheaper.

questions.q: What is the labour variance?
o: J$90,000 under budget, which is favourable
J$290,000 over budget, which is adverse
J$90,000 over budget, which is favourable
J$90,000 over budget, which is adverse
questions.why: Actual − budget = 1,290,000 − 1,200,000 = J$90,000 over. A cost over budget is an adverse variance. As a percentage it is 90,000 ÷ 1,200,000 = 7.5% over.

questions.q: By what percentage is transport over budget?
o: About 13%
About 27%
About 15%
About 11.5%
questions.why: Variance = 207,000 − 180,000 = J$27,000. 27,000 ÷ 180,000 × 100 = 15%. Dividing by the actual instead of the budget gives about 13%.

questions.q: What should Tanya say about the J$150,000 materials saving?
o: Probably not a saving: the delayed luminaires are not yet bought
It is a real saving that can be spent on the transport overspend
It shows the crew is using less cable, so the estimates can be cut
It proves the materials budget was set too high and must be cut
questions.why: A favourable variance needs checking too. Two jobs are waiting for luminaires that have not arrived, so their materials have not been bought or invoiced; the cost will appear later. Treating it as a saving would mislead the manager.

questions.q: Which line is the best way to report the transport overspend?
o: Transport is J$27,000 (15%) over, so drivers must use less fuel and plan routes better
Transport is over budget again this month; the manager should look into why and decide
Transport J$27,000 (15%) over: 12 extra wholesaler trips; propose van stock lists and checks
Transport cost J$207,000 against a budget of J$180,000, which is more than it should cost
questions.why: A good variance report gives the figure, the cause and a proposed action, so the manager can decide quickly. Blame, vague statements and bare numbers do not help.

questions.q: The sick electrician is the only person trained on the fire alarm system, and the risk register scored this risk at 2 × 4 = 8 in January, with no control. What lesson should the register now record?
o: Raise the consequence to 5 so the score is higher next time
Add a control: train a second person on fire alarms before such jobs
Remove the risk, because sickness cannot be planned for
Lower the likelihood to 1, since it has happened and will not happen again
questions.why: A risk register is useful only if each risk has a control that reduces its chance or its harm. Having a second trained person removes the single point of failure; a scoring change on its own changes nothing on the ground.

questions.q: What should Jerome do first about the supermarket's request to start two weeks early?
o: Agree at once, because the supermarket is a valuable client
Refuse, because the plan was fixed in January and cannot change
Get the new dates and scope in writing, then check for clashes
Move the school job later without telling the school, to make room for it
questions.why: A change is managed, not just accepted or refused: confirm it in writing, check clashes and labour hours, check material lead times, list and cost the options, and take them to the manager. Other clients are told before their jobs move.

questions.q: The school's switchboard will be three weeks late. Which is a contingency, rather than a control, for this risk?
o: Ordering switchboards as soon as a job is confirmed
Confirming delivery with the supplier each week
Keeping a second approved supplier's prices on file
Re-sequencing the school job to do other work first
questions.why: A control acts in advance to make the risk less likely or less harmful; a contingency is what you do once the risk has happened. Re-sequencing the job now, so the crew stays productive while waiting, is the contingency. The other three are controls for next time.

questions.q: It is June. Which risk should Jerome make sure is on the register and controlled before August?
o: Too many trainees asking for work placements with the crew
Storms and hurricanes stopping site work and delaying deliveries
Clients paying their invoices earlier than the contract requires
The cost of printer paper for job sheets rising during the year
questions.why: The hurricane season runs from June to November, with August to October the busiest. The plan should schedule outdoor work early, keep stock, prepare the vans and stores, and have a plan for securing sites and for priority repairs afterwards.

questions.q: What are the crew's completion rate and first-time pass rate this month?
questions.why: Completion: 36 ÷ 40 × 100 = 90%. First-time pass: 19 ÷ 20 × 100 = 95%. Both are rates of the number done against the number planned or inspected.

questions.q: What are the callback rate and the rate of fitting light points?
o: 5% and 3 points an hour
4% and 3 points an hour
4% and 0.33 points an hour
25% and 2.5 points an hour
questions.why: Callbacks: 5 ÷ 125 × 100 = 4%. Rate of work: 96 points ÷ 32 hours = 3 points an hour. Dividing the wrong way round gives 0.33, and using the wrong base gives the other figures.

questions.q: Halfway through the next month, 30% of the month's jobs are complete. What should Jodi-Ann do?
o: Nothing yet, as the crew often catches up in the last week
Look at the job sheets for the cause and agree an action now
Lower the month's target so the completion rate looks right
Warn the crew that their pay will be cut if the month is missed
questions.why: With half the time gone and under a third of the work done, the crew is behind. The job sheets show whether the cause is late materials, rework, sickness or wrong estimates; an action with an owner and date is agreed now, and anything beyond her authority is reported with the figures.

questions.q: How should Jodi-Ann answer the suggestion to leave two small callbacks off the log?
o: Agree, since very small callbacks do not affect the KPI's meaning
Agree this month only, as the rate is already close to its target
Log them under a different heading so the rate is not affected
Refuse: the log must be complete, or the real cause stays hidden
questions.why: KPIs are only useful if the data is honest and collected the same way every time. Two hidden callbacks make the rate look better and hide a workmanship problem that could grow. The log records every callback, however small.

questions.q: An electrical contractor's monthly costs include workshop rent, cable bought for each job, insurance and fuel for each site visit. Which two are fixed costs?
o: Rent and insurance
Cable and fuel
Rent and cable
Insurance and fuel
questions.why: Fixed costs stay the same whatever the amount of work done: rent and insurance are paid whether the crew does five jobs or fifty. Cable and fuel rise and fall with the work, so they are variable costs.
